notes: Attorney General reference on unduly lenient conditional discharge for child cruelty; discretion not to increase sentence is clear.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference: unduly lenient conditional discharge for child cruelty
key_facts: Franklin Mokaki pleaded guilty to two counts of cruelty to her 11-year-old son, including assaults with a rolling pin and coat hanger and abandonment at a supermarket.
Snaresbrook Crown Court imposed a two-year conditional discharge on each count on the basis of a written plea.
At the reference hearing the two younger children were progressing toward reunification with their parents under care proceedings.
The Court of Appeal considered that custody of about 18 months would have been appropriate but declined to interfere for the children's sake.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 against an unduly lenient non-custodial sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; sentence held unduly lenient but not increased; conditional discharge left undisturbed in the exercise of discretion.
enrichment.ratio: A conditional discharge for sustained child cruelty causing injury was unduly lenient and merited custody, but the Court of Appeal may refuse to increase sentence where double jeopardy, prior liberty, and the welfare of remaining children in reunification make immediate imprisonment disproportionate.
legal_issues: Whether a conditional discharge adequately reflected the gravity of child cruelty offences
Whether the Court of Appeal should substitute a custodial term despite double jeopardy
Impact of ongoing public law care proceedings on sentencing discretion

notes: Police disciplinary immunity and absolute privilege analysis against sex discrimination claims is detailed; Neuberger LJ dissent on board composition is noted.

enrichment.short_title: Sex discrimination immunity in police disciplinary proceedings
key_facts: Diane Heath, a civilian station reception officer, alleged sexual assault by a police inspector and later complained that a three-man Police Disciplinary Board discriminated against her at the disciplinary hearing.
Her complaints included an all-male board, difficulty obtaining female support in the hearing room, and humiliating cross-examination without intervention by the board.
The Employment Tribunal and Employment Appeal Tribunal held they had no jurisdiction because absolute privilege attached to quasi-judicial disciplinary proceedings.
Neuberger LJ would have allowed part of the appeal relating to the Commissioner's selection of an all-male board.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal upholding lack of jurisdiction over sex discrimination claims arising from police disciplinary proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; absolute privilege barred the discrimination claims against board members and the Commissioner.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings before a Police Disciplinary Board under the 1985 Regulations are quasi-judicial; absolute privilege protecting the integrity of such proceedings extends to sex discrimination claims under the Sex Discrimination Act 1975, and challenges to a board's composition are for the board itself to rule upon.
legal_issues: Whether judicial immunity extends beyond defamation to discrimination claims
Whether police disciplinary hearings are quasi-judicial proceedings
Whether absolute privilege bars Employment Tribunal claims of unlawful discrimination during disciplinary hearings
Whether selection of an all-male disciplinary board gives rise to a freestanding discrimination claim
linked_authorities: R v Home Secretary ex p Leech (No 2) [1994] QB 198

confidence.notes: Core immunity reasoning and outcome are clear; dissent on board composition is secondary.

notes: Exceptional HIV pregnancy Article 3 asylum case; section 101 IAT jurisdiction analysis is central and well reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: HIV-positive mother's Article 3 appeal on unborn child risk
key_facts: A Ghanaian woman with HIV succeeded before an adjudicator on Article 3 only because removal during pregnancy would risk HIV transmission to her unborn child.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal by treating later medical evidence as decisive and finding perversity.
The child was born HIV-free by caesarean before the IAT hearing.
Laws LJ held the IAT had no jurisdiction to substitute a merits decision without first finding error of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an IAT decision restoring removal after an adjudicator allowed an Article 3 human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT order set aside and adjudicator's decision restored; anonymity order made; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under sections 101 and 102 of the 2002 Act the IAT's jurisdiction is confined to points of law and Ravichandran does not apply; the adjudicator's Article 3 finding based on risk to the unborn child was not perverse, and the mother's suffering from witnessing preventable HIV infection in a newborn can engage Article 3.
legal_issues: Scope of IAT appellate jurisdiction under section 101 after the 2002 Act
Whether Article 3 can succeed on risk to an unborn child where the mother has treatment abroad
Whether the adjudicator's decision was perverse
Application of N v SSHD to resource-based Article 3 claims
linked_authorities: Ravichandran (1996) IAR 97
N v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 1 WLR 1182
Subesh v SSHD [2004] EWCA Civ 56

notes: Procedural unfairness in ancillary relief summary dismissal is straightforward; facts and remedy are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Procedural unfairness in ancillary relief summary dismissal
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Taylor's consent orders required sale of optician businesses and limited the husband's drawings to £1,500 per month pending sale.
The wife applied for disclosure and an injunction over suspected breaches; a without-notice injunction was later discharged and her application summarily dismissed.
The judge treated the wife's implementation application as a company law dispute with the selling agent rather than ancillary relief enforcement.
No formal summary dismissal application had been issued and the wife had insufficient time to respond to new evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against summary dismissal of an ancillary relief implementation and disclosure application.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; appeal allowed; summary dismissal set aside and application remitted to the county court.
enrichment.ratio: It was procedurally unfair to summarily dismiss an ancillary relief implementation application without notice of that course and without opportunity to reply; alleged breaches of consent undertakings on drawings and company assets are matters for the ancillary relief court, not a separate uncommenced company claim.
legal_issues: Whether summary dismissal without a formal application was procedurally fair
Whether enforcement of consent ancillary relief orders belongs in the family court
Whether disputes about the selling agent displaced the husband's alleged breaches

notes: Major misfeasance in public office and constitutional rights judgment; exemplary damages remitted but liability analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Misfeasance actionable without proof of damage for prison mail breach
key_facts: Jeffrey Watkins, a life prisoner, sued prison officers for misfeasance after legal correspondence was opened in breach of Rule 37A.
The trial judge found bad faith by three officers but held no actionable damage was proved and dismissed the claim.
Brooke and Laws LJJ held interference with access to courts is a constitutional right protected like the right to vote in Ashby v White.
Nominal damages of £5 were awarded and exemplary damages remitted to the trial judge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court judgment dismissing a prisoner's misfeasance in public office claim for want of proved damage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; nominal general damages entered against three officers; case remitted on exemplary damages.
enrichment.ratio: Misfeasance in public office is complete without proof of special damage where a public officer maliciously interferes with a constitutional right such as unimpeded access to the courts and legal advisers; proof of economic loss is required in the other class of case.
legal_issues: Whether misfeasance in public office is actionable per se
Whether proof of damage is always required
Whether breach of Rule 37A can infringe a constitutional right
Appropriate level of exemplary damages against individual prison officers

notes: Split court on reinsurance waiver; affirmation reversal and damages figure are explicit in the order.

enrichment.short_title: Cargo reinsurance: waiver split but affirmation avoids contract
key_facts: London reinsurers avoided a facultative cargo reinsurance after undisclosed shipments of Rolex and other high-value watches for a Cancun retailer.
The slip described valuable regular shipments of clocks from Miami; the reinsurers said watches were material and misrepresented.
Peter Gibson LJ cast the deciding vote: waiver appeal dismissed 2-1 but affirmation appeal allowed 2-1.
Notice of cancellation given in April 2001 was held to affirm the contract; judgment was entered for the reinsured for $666,216.96 plus interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Commercial Court trial on misrepresentation, non-disclosure, waiver, inducement, and affirmation in a reinsurance dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on affirmation only; judge's order set aside; reinsurers' claim dismissed; judgment for reinsured on counterclaim; 50% costs.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual notice of cancellation can affirm a reinsurance contract if given with knowledge of the right to avoid; contemporaneous email evidence that the underwriter received notice without repudiating it undermined the trial judge's contrary finding, while the majority upheld that describing clocks on the slip did not put reinsurers on inquiry so as to waive non-disclosure of watches.
legal_issues: Whether reinsurers waived non-disclosure by failing to inquire about clocks on the slip
Whether notice of cancellation amounted to affirmation of the contract
Whether the Court of Appeal could overturn findings on affirmation
Whether non-disclosure of Rolex watches induced the underwriter

notes: Complex joint venture and charge agreement construction; partial set-aside quantum and anti-suit injunction holdings are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Enron charge agreement default judgments partly set aside
key_facts: Enron entered default judgments of about US$8.1m against chargors under a share charge guaranteeing TBNG liabilities under a Turkish hydrocarbon joint venture agreement.
Closing under the JVA never occurred though Enron exercised its option; TBNG and defendants disputed loan repayment and commenced Texas fraud proceedings.
Langley J held estoppel and closure defences failed but quantum defences on unreimbursed payments and revenue set-off had real prospects.
Default judgments were set aside only as to disputed quantum; anti-suit injunction granted and stay refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to set aside default judgments, stay proceedings pending arbitration, and grant an anti-suit injunction restraining Texas proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Partial set-aside on quantum only; substantial principal of about $2.29m remained due; stay refused; anti-suit injunction granted.
enrichment.ratio: Personal guarantors under an absolute English-law charge covenant remain liable for defined secured liabilities without TBNG set-off rights being excluded only by express terms; estoppel could not establish closing where both parties treated closing as future, but set-off and inclusion of unreinvoiced capex gave a real prospect of reducing quantum.
legal_issues: Whether default judgments should be set aside under CPR 13.2 and 13.3
Whether closing occurred so as to trigger repayment obligations
Whether chargors could rely on TBNG set-offs against secured liabilities
Whether proceedings should be stayed or Texas litigation restrained

notes: Libel meaning tiers and repetition rule discussion; Hartwell strike-out upheld, Jameel meaning restored for jury.

enrichment.short_title: Sunday Times Bin Laden link article: Chase level-2 meaning restored
key_facts: The Sunday Times published an article linking Saudi businessman Yousef Jameel to September 11 litigation and the Golden Chain donor list.
Gray J struck out Hartwell PLC's claim and limited Mr Jameel's action to a lower Chase meaning of grounds to inquire rather than reasonable grounds to suspect.
The Court of Appeal held the article was arguably capable of a level-2 Chase meaning despite mitigating passages.
Hartwell's appeal failed because no reasonable reader would defame the company through association alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from summary disposal and meaning rulings in libel claims arising from a Sunday Times article.
enrichment.outcome: Mr Jameel's appeal allowed on meaning; Hartwell appeal dismissed; action to proceed on alternative Chase meanings; repetition rule point left unresolved.
enrichment.ratio: Where a publication arguably suggests reasonable grounds to suspect serious misconduct, it is for a jury not a judge to decide between Chase level-2 and level-3 meanings unless the antidote unequivocally negates the sting; a company is not defamed merely because its proprietor is slurred unless corporate wrongdoing or investigation is imputed.
legal_issues: Whether the article bore a Chase level-2 meaning of reasonable grounds to suspect terrorism funding
Application of the bane and antidote principle
Whether the repetition rule applies to level-3 justification
Whether Hartwell PLC was defamed by association with Mr Jameel

notes: Serious section 18 assault with suspended/deferred sentence replaced; jurisdiction over affray sentences clarified at hearing.

enrichment.short_title: AG reference: suspended GBH sentence replaced with two years
key_facts: The offender viciously attacked a vulnerable man in drink, causing permanent eye damage and a penile skin injury including biting through trousers.
He was convicted of section 18 GBH with intent after trial and initially received two years' imprisonment suspended for two years, later deferred for six months.
He had extensive violent convictions, was on licence, and had committed further affrays and weapon offences while on bail.
The Court of Appeal considered at least four years appropriate but substituted two years' immediate custody.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 against an unduly lenient suspended and deferred sentence for section 18 GBH with intent.
enrichment.outcome: Reference upheld; two years' immediate imprisonment substituted for the section 18 offence with concurrent 12-month terms on two affray counts; no separate penalty on other matters.
enrichment.ratio: A suspended or deferred sentence was unduly lenient for a sustained unprovoked section 18 street attack on a vulnerable victim causing lasting injury, especially given the offender's record and licence status; the Court of Appeal will interfere despite treatment progress where the original sentence was far too low.
legal_issues: Whether suspension or deferment was unduly lenient for section 18 GBH with intent
Whether the Court of Appeal should exercise discretion not to increase sentence
Effect of double jeopardy and engagement in aggression treatment programmes
Court's jurisdiction over concurrent affray sentences passed at the same time
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 47 of 1994, R v Smith 16 Cr App R (S) 865

notes: Solicitor negligence trial on Green Belt option trigger; liability finding limited but causation and damages analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor negligence over Green Belt option trigger misunderstanding
key_facts: Mrs Clarke sold Mentone Farm near Heathrow to Ravenseft under a conditional contract and Green Belt option at fixed prices.
She believed the option would trigger on publication of the inspector's report recommending release from the Green Belt, not on formal adoption of the local plan.
The inspector's report was published in November 1998 but adoption did not occur until April 2001 after Secretary of State intervention.
Collins J found Mrs Mawson negligent in failing to correct the client's misunderstanding at a June 1998 meeting but causation and loss were not proved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on liability and causation only in a professional negligence claim against solicitors advising on a conditional sale and Green Belt option.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants entitled only to nominal damages; negligence established in part but no loss of chance or interest claim succeeded.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor advising on a contract whose key trigger is release from the Green Belt must understand the contract's effect and correct a client's mistaken belief that the option period runs from publication of the inspector's report; however, without hindsight the client would still have contracted and had no real chance of negotiating interest or avoiding a fixed-price option.
legal_issues: Scope of a commercial property solicitor's duty regarding planning procedure
Whether the client shared the solicitor's misunderstanding of the trigger event
Whether proper advice would have prevented entry into the contract
Whether Ravenseft would have agreed to interest or a longstop date
Correct measure of loss on a no-transaction case
